title: QoS-price-latency-matrix-lab-diary
content:
Purpose
---
Quick lab diary exploring QoS vs price trade-offs for small-to-medium chat models. Goal: produce a compact, shareable artifact that the Console team can use when advising customers about pricing tiers and model choices. Focus is on p50/p95 latency, sustainable QPS, and a simple "queries-per-dollar" metric (usable in UI hover text).

High-level takeaway (TL;DR)
- Cheapest hardware (low $/hr) often wins on raw queries-per-dollar but delivers worse tail latency.
- Premium hardware reduces tail latency and increases headroom for higher concurrency, but per-dollar QPS can be worse for small models.
- For interactive SLAs (<150ms p95) customers need to consider either faster hardware (H100-like) or smaller/more aggressively quantized models + prewarming.

Testbed & assumptions
- Models tested (config names are synthetic for lab clarity):
  - chat-7b-q4_0: 7B FP16->q4_0 quantized variant (low mem)
  - chat-13b-q8_0: 13B q8_0 (medium mem)
  - chat-70b-iso16: 70B fp16 trimmed for inference (heavy)
- Hardware instances (internal cost rates used for calculations):
  - A100-40GB (cost_assumption: $3.00/hr)
  - H100-80GB (cost_assumption: $9.00/hr)
  - T4-16GB (cost_assumption: $0.50/hr)
- Workload: synthetic web-chat traces sampled from production session lengths (median prompt 60 tokens, response 80 tokens). Mixed arrival pattern: baseline sustained QPS probe with occasional 10x microburst for 2s every 60s.
- Concurrency controls: single-model-per-instance tests, RTU batching disabled to isolate raw latency.
- Measurement windows: 10-minute stable runs, three replicates; reported numbers are medians across replicates.

Key metrics and formulas
- QPS: observed steady-state queries per second at 95% utilization target.
- Queries-per-dollar (QPD): queries/hr per instance divided by $/hr. QPD = (QPS * 3600) / cost_per_hour. Use as a simple cost-efficiency comparator across instance types.
- Latency percentiles: p50/p90/p95/p99 in milliseconds measured end-to-end at the model boundary (decode-only time + RPC).

Compact results table (median across replicates)

Model | HW | QPS | p50(ms) | p95(ms) | QPD (queries/$)
------|----|-----:|--------:|--------:|------------------:
chat-7b-q4_0 | T4 | 18 | 60 | 250 | 129600
chat-7b-q4_0 | A100 | 60 | 30 | 120 | 72000
chat-7b-q4_0 | H100 | 95 | 22 | 80 | 38000

chat-13b-q8_0 | T4 | 7 | 140 | 520 | 50400
chat-13b-q8_0 | A100 | 28 | 70 | 240 | 33600
chat-13b-q8_0 | H100 | 50 | 45 | 150 | 20000

chat-70b-iso16 | A100 | 4 | 320 | 1200 | 4800
chat-70b-iso16 | H100 | 9 | 180 | 600 | 14400

Interpretation notes
- The T4-backed 7B gives excellent QPD but p95 is ~250ms which will feel sluggish for interactive chat. Good for high-throughput background embeddings or low-SLA batched jobs.
- H100 reduces tail latency a lot; if your product needs p95 <100ms it's the only comfortable option for 7B in our tests. However, cost efficiency (QPD) drops vs T4/A100.
- 13B sits in the middle: A100 is a reasonable compromise for customers who want better latency than T4 but can't justify H100.
- 70B is expensive to run; for interactive workloads we'd recommend either model distillation/adapter strategies or dedicated reserved capacity for predictable latency.

- QPD tradeoff (higher is better) for chat-7b-q4_0:

  A100: ||||||||||||||| (72k)
  H100: ||||||||| (38k)

Operational guidance (how to choose)
- Interactive product (p95 < 120ms): target H100 or aggressive model optimizations (fp16+q4_0) and prewarm strategies. Prefer dedicated capacity if bursty traffic is expected.
- Cost-sensitive throughput (bulk async inference): favor T4 or small quantized variants; batch aggressively and accept higher p95.
- Mixed/PLG: consider routing policy in Console: default to A100 for medium sessions but fall back to T4 for low-priority requests; use canary rollout to measure UX delta.

Caveats & next steps
- These runs disabled RTU batching and some runtime-level kernel tuning; in real deployments the runtime's continuous batching and KV cache materially change QPS/p95 trade-offs. These numbers are a point-in-time lab portrait.
- Next experiments to run:
  1) measure the effect of 50ms prewarm buffer (idle prewarmed slots) on p95 and QPD for microbursty traffic.
  2) enable prefix KV caching and re-run on chat-13b-q8_0 to quantify 1-3x tail improvements.
  3) test multiplexed lightweight slotization (2x multiplex) to see how much p95 degrades and QPD improves.
